questions.question: Two 5.9 m long current-carrying conductors are placed parallel to each other and separated by a distance of 19 cm. One conductor carries a current of 4.2 A and the other carries a current of 6.8 A. Which of the following is the magnitude of the force acting on each conductor?
questions.answer: $\dfrac Fl=\dfrac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{2\pi r}=\dfrac{(4\pi\times10^{-7})(4.2)(6.8)}{2\pi(0.19)}=3.01\times10^{-5}$ N m$^{-1}$, so $F=3.01\times10^{-5}\times5.9=1.77\times10^{-4}$ N (D). B is the force per metre.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT stated by Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion?
questions.answer: A, B and D are Kepler's first, third and second laws. Nothing in Kepler's laws refers to the orientation of the orbital planes relative to the Sun's equator (C).
options: All planets move about the Sun in elliptical orbits where the Sun is at one of the foci.
The ratio of the square of the orbital period to the cube of the mean distances from the Sun is a constant for any planets orbiting the Sun.
The planes in which the planets move about the Sun is parallel to the plane of the equator of the Sun.
A radial distance joining any planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal lengths of time.

questions.question: The diagram shows the spectra of radiation from two objects A and B with their peak intensity occurring at the same wavelength. Let $T_A$ and $T_B$ be the surface temperature of A and B respectively. Which of the following is correct?
questions.answer: By Wien's law, $\lambda_{max}=\dfrac bT$. The same peak wavelength means the same surface temperature (B). The difference in height is due to a different surface area (or emissivity), not temperature.
options: There is insufficient information to compare $T_A$ and $T_B$

questions.question: The diagram shows an ideal step-down transformer. Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.answer: For an ideal transformer $V_pI_p=V_sI_s$. A step-down transformer has $V_s<V_p$, so $I_s>I_p$ (C). The dotted line shows the magnetic flux path, not an eddy current; the core links the coils magnetically (not electrically); and a DC supply gives no changing flux, so no emf is induced in the secondary.
options: The dotted line indicates the path of the eddy current.
The soft iron core provides an electrical connection between the primary and the secondary coil.
The current in the primary coil is lower than that in the secondary coil.
The transformer will function the same if the AC supply is replaced by a constant DC supply.

questions.question: Which of the following can produce the spectrum shown?
questions.answer: The graph has intense narrow peaks at specific wavelengths: an emission line spectrum. Only a gas discharge tube gives this. An incandescent bulb, a candle flame and sunlight (a continuous spectrum, with dark absorption lines) give broad continuous spectra (A).
options: The spectrum from a gas discharge tube
The spectrum from an incandescent light bulb
The spectrum from a burning candle

questions.question: Unpolarised light of intensity $I_0$ passes through two polarising filters A and B before arriving at a screen. The polarising axes of A and B differ by $24^\circ$. Which of the following gives the intensity of the light arriving at the screen in terms of $I_0$?
questions.answer: After A: $\dfrac{I_0}2$. Malus' law: $I=\dfrac{I_0}2\cos^224^\circ=0.42I_0$ (A).

questions.question: The diagram shows a simple DC motor. Which of the following is the reason why the magnitude of the torque acting on a DC motor varies with time?
questions.answer: The force $F=BIl$ on side AB is constant, because AB is always perpendicular to the (radial) field. As the coil rotates, the perpendicular distance from the line of action of the force to the axle changes, so $\tau=r_\perp F$ varies (B).
options: The magnitude of the force acting on AB varies with time.
The perpendicular distance between the force acting on AB and the axle varies with time.
The voltage supply to the DC motor varies with time.
The strength of the magnetic field provided by the magnets varies with time.

questions.question: When monochromatic light passes through a diffraction grating, a pattern of bright fringes is formed on a viewing screen. Which of the following arrangements would produce the greatest angle $\theta$ between the central and first order bright fringes?
questions.answer: $d\sin\theta=m\lambda$, so $\sin\theta=\dfrac{m\lambda}d$. A larger angle needs a smaller slit spacing $d$ (more lines per mm) and a longer wavelength. 600 lines per mm and yellow light (longer wavelength than violet) give the greatest $\theta$ (D).

questions.question: The information about a nuclear reaction is given: $^2_1\text{H}+{}^3_1\text{H}\to{}^4_2\text{He}+{}^1_0\text{n}+$ energy released. Masses: $^2_1$H 2.014102 u, $^3_1$H 3.016049 u, $^4_2$He 4.002602 u, $^1_0$n 1.008665 u. What is the energy released in this reaction?
The magnetic flux through a coil over time is recorded by the graph shown. Which of the following graphs best represents how the magnitude of the induced emf varies over the same period?
questions.answer: Faraday's law: $|\varepsilon|=N\left|\dfrac{\Delta\phi}{\Delta t}\right|$, the magnitude of the gradient of the flux graph. From 0 to $t_1$ the flux rises at a constant rate, and from $t_1$ to $t_2$ it falls at about the same rate (magnitude), so the emf has constant magnitude from 0 to $t_2$. It is zero from $t_2$ to $t_3$ (flux constant), then a small constant value from $t_3$ to $t_4$ (gentle constant gradient) (A).

questions.question: A charged particle P enters a magnetic field of strength 0.422 mT perpendicular to the field with a speed of $2.675\times10^6\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. The particle follows a semi-circular path and arrives at a detector 262 m from where it entered the magnetic field. Which of the following is the correct mass and charge of P?
questions.answer: The field is out of the page, the particle moves left and is deflected downwards. For a positive charge the force $q\mathbf v\times\mathbf B$ would be upwards, so the charge is negative. The diameter is 262 m, so $r=131$ m. $qvB=\dfrac{mv^2}r$ gives $r=\dfrac{mv}{qB}$. Testing D: $r=\dfrac{(6.644\times10^{-27})(2.675\times10^6)}{(3.204\times10^{-19})(0.422\times10^{-3})}=131$ m. This matches (D). (A and B give $r\approx0.02$ m.)

questions.question: A stroboscopic camera with a frequency of 2.00 Hz captured part of a projectile's motion before it malfunctioned. The images captured by the camera are shown in the graph. If the initial speed of projection is $45.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, which of the following is closest to the angle of projection of the projectile?
questions.answer: The images are 0.50 s apart and the horizontal spacing is about 9.5 m, so $v_x\approx19\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (constant). $\cos\theta=\dfrac{v_x}{u}=\dfrac{19}{45}=0.42$, so $\theta\approx65^\circ$ (C).

questions.question: A small bar magnet is attached to the rotating shaft of a motor and a coil is placed directly under the magnet. The starting position of the magnet is shown. As the magnet rotates (anticlockwise as shown), the induced emf across the coil is recorded and shown in the graph. Which of the following is the position of the magnet at $t_1$?
questions.answer: The graph shows that $t_1$ is at the minimum of the sine curve, three quarters of the way through a cycle. The magnet rotates anticlockwise from N pointing up, through N left (1/4), N down (1/2), to N pointing right (3/4), as in C.

questions.question: A group of students uses the apparatus shown to determine the wavelength of the monochromatic light emitted from a discharge tube behind a narrow slit. A diffraction grating is placed at the end of the ruler and the students observe the diffracted image of the first order fringe. They move the pin P to align with the first order fringe and measure the distance $x$. Which of the following would improve the accuracy of the results?
questions.answer: The second order fringe is further from the central position, so the measured distance is larger and the same ruler uncertainty is a smaller fraction of it; this improves accuracy (D). Raising the voltage does not change the wavelength; repeating the experiment improves reliability/precision (it does not remove a systematic error); shorter rulers would not reach the fringe.
options: Increase the voltage supplied to the discharge tube.
Replace the two 1 m rulers with 30 cm rulers of the same scale.
Measure the position of the second order bright fringe instead of the first order.

questions.question: An aeroplane with a wingspan of 37.8 m is flying at a speed of $230\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ parallel to the Earth's surface. It travels through an area with a magnetic field strength of $4.59\times10^{-5}$ T. The magnetic field makes an angle of $25^\circ$ to the vertical. Which of the following is the induced emf between the ends of the aeroplane's wings?
questions.answer: Only the vertical component of the field is cut by the horizontal wings: $\varepsilon=B\cos25^\circ\times l\times v=(4.59\times10^{-5})(\cos25^\circ)(37.8)(230)=0.36$ V (B).

questions.question: A laser is positioned inside a space capsule exactly half-way between two emergency hatches P and Q. The hatches open automatically when light from the laser reaches them. The capsule travels past a scientist on Earth at a constant speed of $0.7c$ (towards Q) and the laser is switched on at the exact time it passes the scientist. Which of the following best describes the observation made by the scientist?
questions.answer: In the scientist's frame light travels at $c$ in both directions (second postulate), but hatch P is moving towards the light and hatch Q is moving away from it. The light reaches P first, so P opens before Q (A). (For observers in the capsule they open simultaneously: simultaneity is relative.)

questions.question: A particle P is placed at a height $h$ above the ground on a loop-the-loop track. The radius of the loop is $r$. If P is released from rest, what is the minimum value of $h$ in order for P to complete the loop?
questions.answer: Conservation of energy from release to the top of the loop (height $2r$): $\tfrac12mv^2=mg(h-2r)$, so $v^2=2g(h-2r)$. At the top, the minimum condition is that the normal force is zero, so gravity alone provides the centripetal force: $mg=\dfrac{mv^2}r$, i.e. $v^2=gr$. Then $2g(h-2r)=gr$, so $h=2.5r$ (B).

questions.question: The gravitational force $F$ acting on a planet due to the Sun's gravitational field varies with the planet's distance $r$ from the centre of the Sun as shown in the graph. Which of the following quantities of the planet is given by the area under the graph between X and Y?
questions.answer: The area under a force against distance graph is $\int F\,dr$, the work done by the force (a force multiplied by a distance, not by a time, so not an impulse). Work done by the field equals the negative of the change in gravitational potential energy, so the area gives the magnitude of the change in gravitational potential energy (B).
options: The impulse of the gravitational force
The change in the gravitational potential energy

questions.question: A proton enters a region of uniform electric field formed by two parallel charged plates with a potential difference of 25 V separated by $2.3\times10^{-2}$ m. The proton enters the electric field $6.5\times10^{-3}$ m below the positive plate and exits the field $4.1\times10^{-3}$ m above the negative plate. What is the work done on the proton by the electric field?

Astronomers detected an asteroid orbiting Proxima Centauri with a radius of $2.55\times10^{13}$ m. The asteroid was detected because of the small change in velocity of Proxima Centauri as the asteroid orbits it. The graph shows how the component of Proxima Centauri's velocity towards the Earth varied over time. Which of the following is closest to the velocity required for the asteroid to escape Proxima Centauri's gravitational field from its orbit?
questions.answer: The star's velocity oscillates with the period of the asteroid's orbit, which from the graph is $T=19$ days. $v_{orbit}=\dfrac{2\pi r}T=\dfrac{2\pi(2.55\times10^{13})}{19\times86400}=9.76\times10^7\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Escape speed from the orbit is $\sqrt2\,v_{orbit}=1.38\times10^8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (B), since $v_{esc}=\sqrt{2GM/r}$ and $v_{orbit}=\sqrt{GM/r}$.

questions.question: Describe the main differences between the models of light proposed by Newton and Huygens.
questions.answer: Newton proposed that light consists of particles (which he called corpuscles), while Huygens proposed that light is a wave, propagating as wavelets (every point on a wavefront acting as a source of secondary wavelets).

questions.question: In 1801, Thomas Young conducted his famous double slit experiment. Explain which model of light was supported by his experimental results.
questions.answer: When light was shone on a double slit, an interference pattern of alternating bright and dark fringes formed on a distant screen. Light from the two slits (diffracted at each slit) travels different distances to a point on the screen. Where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths ($n\lambda$) the waves arrive in phase and interfere constructively, producing a bright fringe. Where the path difference is $\left(n+\tfrac12\right)\lambda$ the waves arrive out of phase and interfere destructively, producing a dark fringe. Interference and diffraction can only be explained by waves, so the experiment supported Huygens' wave model of light.

questions.question: Two identical masses of 26.5 kg are placed with their centres separated by a distance of $d$ m. Given that $d=11.0$ m, calculate the gravitational force between the two masses.

Describe the graph of the gravitational force between the two masses as they are separated, and state the magnitudes of the force when the separation of the centres is $2d$ and $4d$ (as a sketch of force against separation). Take $d=11.0$ m.
questions.answer: The graph is an inverse-square curve: it decreases steeply and levels off, approaching the separation axis without touching it ($F\propto 1/r^2$). At $d$: $3.87\times10^{-10}$ N. At $2d$ the force is $\tfrac14$ of this: $9.7\times10^{-11}$ N. At $4d$ the force is $\tfrac1{16}$: $2.4\times10^{-11}$ N.

questions.question: A circular coil of diameter 125 mm has 450.0 turns. It is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 85 mT such that its plane is perpendicular to the magnetic field. Calculate the magnetic flux passing through the coil when it is in the position shown.
questions.answer: Flux does not depend on the number of turns. $\phi=BA\cos\theta=(85\times10^{-3})\left[\pi\left(\dfrac{0.125}2\right)^2\right]\cos0^\circ=1.0\times10^{-3}$ Wb.

questions.question: The coil (diameter 125 mm, 450.0 turns, in a uniform field of 85 mT, initially perpendicular to the field) is rotated through $90^\circ$ about the axis XX$'$ in a time of 135 ms. Calculate the average emf induced in the coil during this time.
questions.answer: After a $90^\circ$ rotation the plane of the coil is parallel to the field, so the final flux is zero. $\Delta\phi=0-1.0\times10^{-3}=-1.0\times10^{-3}$ Wb. $\varepsilon=-N\dfrac{\Delta\phi}{\Delta t}=-450.0\times\dfrac{-1.0\times10^{-3}}{135\times10^{-3}}$. The average emf has magnitude about 3.5 V (3.3 V if the rounded flux of $1.0\times10^{-3}$ Wb is used, 3.5 V using the unrounded value $1.04\times10^{-3}$ Wb).

questions.question: Explain how the Hafele-Keating experiment validated Einstein's theory of special relativity.
questions.answer: In the Hafele-Keating experiment, very precise atomic clocks were flown on aeroplanes around the world, one eastward (in the direction of Earth's rotation) and one westward, and compared with identical atomic clocks that stayed on the ground. Atomic clocks were needed because the predicted time differences are tiny. The clocks on the eastward plane recorded less elapsed time, and those on the westward plane more, than the ground clocks, in agreement with the time dilation predicted by Einstein's theory. This was the first experimental validation using macroscopic clocks, confirming that the elapsed time depends on relative motion.

questions.question: Matthew takes a 1.00 metre ruler and sets off in a spaceship. He travels past Anna at a speed of $0.75c$ with the ruler aligned in the direction of travel. Matthew and Anna both measure the length of the ruler at the instant they pass each other. How long does Anna measure the ruler to be?

Matthew measures a 1.00 m ruler travelling with him, and Anna (measuring as he passes at $0.75c$) finds it to be 0.66 m. When Matthew returns, they compare the results of their measurements. How are they able to explain their seemingly contradictory results?
questions.answer: The results are consistent with Einstein's special relativity (length contraction). Matthew is at rest relative to the ruler (in the same inertial frame), so he measures its proper length, 1.00 m. Anna is in a different inertial frame, moving relative to the ruler, so she measures a contracted length, 0.66 m. Neither is wrong: lengths measured in different inertial frames of reference differ, and both frames are equally valid.

questions.question: Mimas is a moon of Saturn and orbits Saturn with a mean radius of $1.86\times10^8$ m and orbital period of 0.942 Earth days. Calculate the mass of Saturn.

Dione is another moon of Saturn and orbits Saturn with a mean radius of $3.78\times10^8$ m. Given that Mimas orbits Saturn with a mean radius of $1.86\times10^8$ m and orbital period of 0.942 Earth days, calculate the orbital period of Dione in Earth days.
questions.answer: Kepler's third law: $\dfrac{r_M^3}{T_M^2}=\dfrac{r_D^3}{T_D^2}$, so $\dfrac{(1.86\times10^8)^3}{(0.942)^2}=\dfrac{(3.78\times10^8)^3}{T_D^2}$, giving $T_D=2.73$ Earth days.

questions.question: Dione orbits Saturn in an elliptical orbit. Explain why the orbital velocity of Dione changes as it orbits Saturn.
questions.answer: In an elliptical orbit Dione's distance from Saturn's centre changes, so its gravitational potential energy changes. By conservation of energy the total energy is constant, so a change in gravitational potential energy results in an equal and opposite change in kinetic energy, and hence in speed. When Dione is closest to Saturn its potential energy is lowest and its speed is greatest; when it is furthest away its speed is lowest (consistent with Kepler's second law: equal areas swept in equal times).

questions.question: Coin A is placed on a rotating disc at 1.35 m from the centre of the disc. It has a mass of 15.0 g. The disc begins to rotate and when the frequency of rotation reaches 2.5 Hz, the coin flies off the disc. Give a reason for why Coin A flies off the disc.
questions.answer: The friction between the coin and the disc provides the centripetal force. At this speed the friction needed exceeds the maximum (limiting) friction available, so it can no longer keep the coin moving in a circle, and the coin moves off along a tangent.

questions.question: Coin A (mass 15.0 g) is at 1.35 m from the centre of a rotating disc. Calculate the centripetal force experienced by Coin A just before it flies off, when the frequency of rotation is 2.5 Hz.

Coin A is placed back in its original position, 1.35 m from the centre of a rotating disc. Another identical coin, Coin B, is placed on the same disc closer to the centre. The disc begins to rotate. Explain which coin will fly off the disc first.
questions.answer: Both coins are on the same disc, so they have the same period and angular velocity. Coin A is further from the centre, so it has a greater speed ($v=2\pi r/T$) and needs a greater centripetal force ($F_c=m\omega^2r$). The coins are identical, so the maximum friction force available is the same for each. Coin A reaches the limiting friction first, so Coin A will fly off first.

questions.question: The diagrams show the key components of two devices, a dynamo torch and an AC induction motor. A dynamo torch operates by squeezing the handle continuously, which causes a permanent magnet to rotate near a fixed coil inside the torch. Compare the physics principles that allow the two devices to operate. In your answer, make reference to the conservation of energy and the components of the devices.
questions.answer: Dynamo torch: squeezing the handle rotates the permanent magnet, so the magnetic flux linking the fixed coil changes continuously. By Faraday's law an emf is induced in the coil, and the current produced lights the bulb. By Lenz's law the induced current produces a magnetic field that opposes the change in flux (the rotation of the magnet), so work must be done by the hand: mechanical (kinetic) energy is converted to electrical energy, consistent with conservation of energy. AC induction motor: the stationary electromagnets of the stator are supplied with AC currents that are out of phase with each other, which creates a rotating magnetic field. The rotor (conducting loops or bars, with no electrical connection to the supply) sees a changing flux, so by Faraday's law currents are induced in it. By Lenz's law these currents oppose the change in flux, so the rotor is made to follow the rotating field. The induced currents in the rotor are in the stator's magnetic field, so by the motor effect the rotor experiences a torque and rotates. Electrical energy is converted to kinetic energy (with some lost as heat). Comparison: both depend on electromagnetic induction (Faraday's and Lenz's laws) and on a rotating magnetic field relative to a conductor. The dynamo (a generator) converts kinetic to electrical energy, while the induction motor converts electrical to kinetic energy. The torch has a rotating permanent magnet and a fixed coil, while the induction motor has fixed electromagnets (stator) producing a rotating field and a rotating coil/rotor in which the current is induced, and the motor also relies on the motor effect.

questions.question: KPLO is a satellite of mass 678.0 kg in a circular orbit about the Moon. Define gravitational potential of an object at a point in a gravitational field.
questions.answer: The gravitational potential at a point is the gravitational potential energy per unit mass at that point, $V=\dfrac Um=-\dfrac{GM}r$: the work done per unit mass in bringing a small mass from infinity (where $V=0$) to that point. (The school's marking guide describes this as work done by the field; the potential is negative, since the field does positive work and the zero is at infinity.)

questions.question: KPLO is a satellite of mass 678.0 kg in a circular orbit about the Moon. Point A is a point in KPLO's orbit and point B is a point on the surface of the Moon. Given that the gravitational potential energy of KPLO at A is 95% of its gravitational potential energy at B and the gravitational field strength at B is 1.622 N/kg, calculate the gravitational field strength at A.
questions.answer: $U_A=0.95U_B$, so $-\dfrac{GMm}{r_A}=0.95\left(-\dfrac{GMm}{r_B}\right)$, giving $r_A=\dfrac{r_B}{0.95}$. $g=\dfrac{GM}{r^2}$, so $g_A=\dfrac{GM}{(r_B/0.95)^2}=0.95^2g_B=0.9025\times1.622=1.46$ N kg$^{-1}$.

questions.question: At the end of the 1800s scientists recognised that there was a relationship between light and electromagnetism. They began performing experiments which used the apparatus shown (a light source shining on an emitter in a vacuum chamber, a receiver, an ammeter and a variable DC power supply). Discuss how the experimental results could only be explained by the development of a new model of light.
questions.answer: These are the photoelectric effect experiments, whose results could not be explained by the classical wave model, which prompted Einstein's photon (particle) model. Result: a photocurrent is detected only when the frequency of the light is above a threshold value, regardless of the intensity of the light (and the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons depends on the frequency, not the intensity). Wave model: energy is proportional to intensity, so light of high enough intensity should eject electrons at any frequency, and the electrons' energy should increase with intensity. The data contradict this. Photon model: light comes in photons with energy $E=hf$, and each electron absorbs one photon. If the photon energy is below the work function no electron is ejected, however many photons there are (high intensity); if it is above, electrons are ejected with $K_{max}=hf-\phi$, and a greater intensity (more photons) increases the number of electrons, and so the current, not their energy.

questions.question: In a video game, the player fires arrows at a fixed speed of $53.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ from the top of a 45.0 m high castle tower, with the angle of projection $\theta$ adjustable. Assume air resistance is negligible. Show that the angle of projection of the arrow is $72.3^\circ$ if the arrow reaches a maximum height of 175.0 m above the ground.
questions.answer: At maximum height $v_y=0$, and the vertical displacement from the launch point is $175.0-45.0=130.0$ m. $v_y^2=u_y^2+2a_ys$: $0=(53.0\sin\theta)^2+2(-9.8)(130.0)$, so $\sin\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt{2548}}{53.0}=0.9525$ and $\theta=72.3^\circ$.

questions.question: In a video game, the player fires arrows at $53.0\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ to the East from the top of a 45.0 m high castle tower. The target moves around the castle in a circular path of radius 180.0 m in an anti-clockwise direction (viewed from above), and takes 16.0 s to complete one revolution. The target is initially placed South of the castle. Given that the arrow will have a range of 180.0 m when projected at $72.3^\circ$, how long should the player wait before firing the arrow such that it will hit the target?
questions.answer: Time of flight: $s_x=u_xt$, so $180.0=(53.0\cos72.3^\circ)t_f$ and $t_f=11.17$ s. Anticlockwise from South, the target reaches East after a quarter of a revolution: $\tfrac14\times16.0=4.00$ s. Since $t_f>4.00$ s, the arrow cannot hit the target the first time it is East. It must hit it the second time, at $16.0+4.00=20.0$ s. The player must wait $20.0-11.17=8.83$ s.

questions.question: The diagrams show the front view and top view of a moving coil galvanometer. The fixed soft iron cylinder and magnets produce a uniform (radial) magnetic field between the magnets. The coil is able to rotate within this field. A current I flows in the coil in the direction shown. Explain which direction the pointer will move.
questions.answer: The current flows from D to C in the coil. By the motor effect (the right-hand palm rule, with the field from N to S) side DC experiences a downward force. The force on the opposite side is in the opposite direction, so the coil experiences an anticlockwise torque (as seen in the front view), and the pointer moves to the negative part of the scale.

questions.question: The coil of a moving coil galvanometer can be damaged when the galvanometer is transported due to the free rotation of the coil. A student suggests that the terminals of the galvanometer could be connected together to reduce the movement of the coil, which would make it less likely to be damaged. Evaluate the student's suggestion.
questions.answer: The suggestion is valid. If the terminals are connected together, the coil is part of a closed circuit. When the galvanometer is moved and the coil rotates in the magnetic field, the flux through the coil changes, so by Faraday's law an emf and a current are induced. By Lenz's law, the induced current produces a force (motor effect) that opposes the change that caused it, which is the rotation of the coil. This electromagnetic damping reduces the movement of the coil, making damage less likely.

questions.question: A photon of wavelength $6.924\times10^{-12}$ m collides with a stationary electron. What is the original energy of the photon in eV?

A photon collides with a stationary electron. After the collision, the photon travels back in the direction it came from with a greater wavelength. No other particles or photons are produced. Explain why the wavelength of the photon is greater after the collision.
questions.answer: By conservation of energy, the electron gains kinetic energy at the expense of the photon, so the photon loses energy. Since $E=hf$, the photon's frequency decreases. The photon still travels at $c$ ($c=f\lambda$), so a lower frequency means a greater wavelength.

questions.question: A photon of wavelength $6.924\times10^{-12}$ m collides with a stationary electron. After the collision, the photon travels back in the direction it came from with a new wavelength of $9.351\times10^{-12}$ m. No other particles or photons are produced. Calculate the speed of the electron after the collision.
questions.answer: Final photon energy: $f_f=\dfrac{3.00\times10^8}{9.351\times10^{-12}}=3.21\times10^{19}$ Hz, so $E_f=hf_f=2.13\times10^{-14}$ J. By conservation of energy the electron gains $E_e=2.87\times10^{-14}-2.13\times10^{-14}=7.45\times10^{-15}$ J. $\tfrac12m_ev^2=7.45\times10^{-15}$: $v=\sqrt{\dfrac{2(7.45\times10^{-15})}{9.109\times10^{-31}}}=1.28\times10^8\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. (This uses the classical kinetic energy, as in the school's solution; the speed is about $0.43c$, where relativistic effects start to matter.)

questions.question: Two proposals for a new power station to supply electricity to a rural town. Proposal 1: a DC power station (100.0 MW at 25.0 kV) connected by 15 km of transmission lines directly to the factory. Proposal 2: an AC power station (100.0 MW at 25.0 kV) with Transformer 1 stepping up to 500.0 kV for 15 km of transmission lines, then Transformer 2 stepping down to 240 V at the factory. The resistance of the transmission lines in both proposals is $3.21\times10^{-4}\ \Omega\,\text{m}^{-1}$. Assess the efficiency of the two power station proposals for the town and suggest a way to improve the efficiency of each proposal. Your analysis should include power delivered, conservation of energy and the efficiency of the transformer. Include both qualitative and quantitative information.
questions.answer: Line resistance: $R=(3.21\times10^{-4})(15\times10^3)=4.815\ \Omega$. Proposal 1 (DC at 25 kV): $I=\dfrac PV=\dfrac{100.0\times10^6}{25.0\times10^3}=4000$ A. $P_{loss}=I^2R=(4000)^2(4.815)=77.0$ MW. Power delivered $=100.0-77.0=23.0$ MW, an efficiency of about 23%. Proposal 2 (AC, 500 kV): for an ideal transformer $P_{in}=P_{out}$, so $I=\dfrac{100.0\times10^6}{500.0\times10^3}=200$ A. $P_{loss}=(200)^2(4.815)=192.6$ kW. Power delivered $\approx100.0-0.19=99.8$ MW, an efficiency of about 99.8% (for ideal transformers). Comparison: by conservation of energy, the power lost in the lines (as heat) is power not delivered. Stepping up the voltage by a factor of 20 reduces the current by a factor of 20 and the $I^2R$ loss by a factor of 400, so Proposal 2 is far more efficient. Real transformers are not 100% efficient: energy is lost as heat in the windings (resistance), eddy currents and hysteresis in the core, and incomplete flux linkage, so the actual power delivered in Proposal 2 would be a little lower than 99.8 MW. Improvements: Proposal 1 – a transformer cannot be used with DC (there is no changing flux), so reduce the loss by generating at a much higher voltage, or use thicker (lower resistance) cables, or shorten the line, or use AC with transformers. Proposal 2 – use a laminated, high-permeability soft iron core to reduce eddy current and hysteresis losses, thicker windings to reduce heating, or tighter winding to improve flux linkage (or lower resistance transmission lines).
